title: All the stories that got the Qatar paddock talking
excerpt:
After one of the most dramatic races in F1 history on the streets of Las Vegas last time out, the F1 paddock quickly packed up and headed to the Middle East for a desert double – Qatar’s Lusail International Circuit hosting the 2026 season’s penultimate round this weekend ahead of an Abu Dhabi finale. And there was plenty to talk about as the drivers and teams arrived for Thursday’s media duties…

Verstappen vs Russell (again)

Max Verstappen delivered a masterclass at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit some five days ago, coming out on top in a race that featured a whopping 35 lead changes and 352 overtakes – including plenty of wheel-to-wheel moments with George Russell.

This came after a clash between the Red Bull and Mercedes drivers during final practice, which reignited their on-and-off rivalry from the last few seasons.

title: Russell reacts to Verstappen’s Las Vegas comments
excerpt:
George Russell has given his reaction to Max Verstappen’s comments about him following the Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the Briton now looking to switch his focus to the race weekend ahead in Qatar after the “quite amusing” remarks.

The rivalry between the two drivers – which stretches back more than three years – was reignited in Nevada following an incident during third practice, which led to Russell stating that “somebody has got to stand up to that guy” off the back of Verstappen receiving a warning from the stewards.

Race day saw the pair line up alongside each other on the front row of the grid before engaging in a long fight for the lead, with Verstappen continuously retaking P1 whenever he had been briefly overtaken by the Mercedes driver.

Kimi Antonelli later moved ahead of Russell into second place, with the British racer then trying to overtake his team mate in the closing stages – a move that backfired when he locked up and hit the barriers, dropping him down to ninth place while Verstappen took victory up ahead.

Following the race, Verstappen labelled Russell as “so far below my level” and said he had found it “fantastic” to see the Silver Arrows car go off track behind him in his mirrors.

When asked on media day ahead of the Qatar Grand Prix about the situation, Russell suggested that he could see the funny side as he answered: “I don't really have much to say, to be honest.

“It was quite amusing, some of the comments post-race. But at the end of the day, he drove an incredible race and won it, so he can afford to say what he wants really and, from my side, moving on.”

Pushed on whether he wanted to say anything in response to Verstappen’s remarks, the 28-year-old said: “No, not really, to be honest. Not really. At the end of the day, I guess I stand by what I said after practice, but he was the one who went out and won the race.

“I didn't, and I'm sure he had a bit of a laugh about that, and that was reasonably amusing. So, yeah, from my side, [it’s a] new race weekend, try and focus on the driving and move on.”

Russell went on to underline that his focus is on succeeding behind the wheel, adding that “it’s not a war of words off track” and that he respects Verstappen “immensely for his driving talent and everything he's achieved on track, and that's that really”.

The Briton also said of the back and forth between himself and Verstappen: “It is all avoidable, at the end of the day, and it's all a bit unnecessary, and it's not something I'm looking to continue. I'm not looking to have poor relationships with people – that's just not really the type of person I am.”

Verstappen was also quizzed on the situation when speaking to the media in Qatar and – when asked if he approaches his battles with Russell on the track differently to his relationship with him off it – the Red Bull driver responded: “During the race you just try to focus on getting the best result out of it, and everything else that has been said off track has been said.

“There's nothing else to add, and also from my side of course, just happy to win in Vegas.

“It was a really difficult race to get right, and at the same time, Vegas is done, now you're here in Qatar and you just try to have another good weekend where of course we're targeting at least a podium, but we'll just see how that goes.”

title: Leclerc and Hamilton address aftermath of Las Vegas clash
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton have opened up on the mood within Ferrari after they clashed during the Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the former admitting that “we’re all disappointed” despite ongoing efforts to improve their on-track relationship.

Following incidents in Italy and Mexico, the pair made contact when Leclerc attempted a pass on his team mate in Las Vegas, resulting in a 10-second time penalty that dropped the Monegasque to P10 in the final classification.

An unrelated penalty for Hamilton contributed to his own P7 finish and rounded out a frustrating weekend for the Scuderia, especially as both had made significant progress after being eliminated in the second stage of Qualifying.

Although Team Principal Fred Vasseur previously confirmed that he had held talks to address how they race one another, he lamented their "lack of respect” in the “unacceptable” episode – a comment Leclerc readily agreed with.

“Fred had already talked on the radio, telling me he wanted to speak to me before [I went] to the media, so I obviously knew where Fred was standing,” Leclerc explained during media duties in Qatar. “As a driver, you’ve got to accept that.

“As a team, we cannot afford to clash between team mates. I think that is very clear for everyone. For the clash in particular in Las Vegas, I took responsibility. I think there’s tension around that we just need to dissipate and make sure that we look at more positive days in the future. That’s all I’m looking for.

“At the end of the day, we are two very strong drivers that want to finish one ahead of the other. Unfortunately, whether it’s here or Monza or Mexico, there have been a bit too many events lately. We need to find a solution as a team to make sure this kind of thing doesn’t happen again.”

He also admitted that he and Hamilton had already spoken ahead of Round 21 in Qatar, but was reluctant to disclose what “solutions” had been proposed within the team.

“We have a very good relationship outside of the car with Lewis,” he said. “I wouldn’t say the atmosphere is good because obviously we are all disappointed with the situation we find ourselves in.

“At the same time, we’re all grown up and responsible so we’ve got to find a solution. Surely there’s not a super happy feeling at the moment. We are the ones that need to find a solution in order to make that better.

PALMER: Where do Ferrari go from here after Las Vegas clash?

“The only thing that I don’t like seeing is people questioning my integrity to the team, my love for the team. I’ve been in Ferrari since 2019. I think there is nothing clearer than the love I have for the team. I’ll do absolutely everything in order to bring Ferrari back to the top.

“Of course mistakes happen along the way and always will. We just try to minimise them, particularly between team mates. I think it’s more the question mark of that that I have seen going around that hurts me more than anything else. The rest is a lot of noise and it’s not the most enjoyable time, but it’s part of the game and I have to accept that.”

While the titles have already been won by Mercedes and Kimi Antonelli respectively, P2 in the Constructors’ Championship is still to play for. Ferrari currently hold a healthy advantage of 77 points over Red Bull, but as Max Verstappen has clinched four victories in six races, they’re still targeting a clean end to the season.

Hamilton – who has experience with intra-team battles, including an unforgettable one with his Mercedes team mate Nico Rosberg – asserted that securing second place is his main priority in the remaining races, with conversations around the rules of engagement a task for the winter break.

He said: “It's interesting, you work with different people along the way and I had great battles with many different team mates in the past and we always figured things out and ended up moving forward in a positive way, which I've no doubt will be the same with Charles.

“We learn the most when we go through these difficult, challenging phases and times and so naturally through those we try and look to see how we can do things better moving forwards. That's just normal, that's what we do as a team to continue to try and elevate.

“You've got to continuously be evolving and I think sitting and having good, open conversations is only positive for what we're trying to build. I still believe entirely in what we're working towards and the amazing job I think everyone back at the factory has done this year.

“We're going to focus on making sure we maximise these next two weekends because it's key to making sure we get second in the constructors' for the team, and then we'll go away and we'll make improvements on processes, on how we engage and communicate and continue to build on that.”

Asked what Ferrari need to do to avoid similar crises, Hamilton added: “I don't have the answer for that. It's not my job, it's not my role, I'm not going to put together what should happen.

“We'll continue to just have good conversations, I think that's the most important thing. It's for Fred to decide the pathway moving forwards as our leader, and I think he can do that.

“We're still free to race and I think that's the ultimate goal being here. We want to race. But of course we don't want what happened last week to ever happen and so we communicate.

“We do enjoy racing together and we do have a really good relationship. It's obviously intense in the background. On the outside it seems a lot more intense than it really is inside.

“I personally don't feel tension. I love racing and I think it's more built up probably outside than I think inside. I think our goal is to get P2 in the constructors' for the team, so we have to work really well together as a team to deliver those results.”

title: Lindblad left ‘trying to hold back tears’ after Las Vegas spin
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad has conceded that he was left “trying to hold back tears” after a spin forced him to retire whilst running near the front in the Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the Briton having since shared his feelings about what happened in a candid social media post.

Having lined up in P5 on the grid, Lindblad enjoyed a good start to the race and kept himself in the mix with the leading pack. However, as he warmed up his tyres behind the Safety Car a little later on, the Racing Bulls driver lost control of his car and spun out of the running.

The 19-year-old opened up on how he was feeling after the incident in a post shared with his social media followers, in which he stated that “the pain of missing out on something like this, and the endless thoughts of what could have been, will always hurt”, having felt that a podium could be possible.

As the paddock assembled for media day ahead of the Qatar Grand Prix, Lindblad gave a further update as he explained: “I feel a bit better. I've tried not to think about it too much.

“It was not an easy flight back – it was quite upsetting afterwards honestly, and I think I tried to be genuine with what I said afterwards but I've tried not to think about it too much. I think it's a bit of a longer thing that will hurt, so just trying to focus on this week now.”

When asked what had led him to speak so honestly on social media, the British driver recalled how he was feeling on the flight out of Las Vegas.

“I was on the flight back and I was pretty emotional, honestly,” said Lindblad. “Being completely frank, there were times I was on the flight and I was just trying to hold back some tears.

“I wanted to write about how I was feeling and, I don't know, I was having these ideas when I was in the shower about how, if I was to tell someone about the weekend and how I was feeling, how I would phrase it, and then in the end I was just feeling this way and wanted to almost get it out.

“I ended up just going on Notes and writing about how I was feeling, and how it all felt and why I felt that way. Then it ended up being quite a cohesive couple of paragraphs and I thought I'd just use that.

“I also want to be quite genuine on my socials. I am quite young and I try not to be too involved in it, but also I'm at that age where I think it's normal to have a bit of involvement and I try to be quite genuine with my page about who I am and stuff, so I thought it was only suitable to be honest.”

Looking ahead to the final two rounds of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, Lindblad is keen to get back behind the wheel and try to secure P5 for Racing Bulls in the Teams’ Championship.

“I think it will be fun – two very different challenges, which I'm looking forward to after Vegas,” he explained. “The race was very fun, but the track was interesting!

“I'm looking forward to these two – it's going to be two proper tracks. I think it's going to be cool, it's going to be fast. It’s been a while since we've been at such a fast track, so I’m just looking forward to getting back in the car.”

title: Camara reacts to decision to sacrifice F2 title challenge
excerpt:
Rafael Camara has admitted that he feels “a bit sad” to be missing the final two rounds of the Formula 2 campaign, with Haas recently confirming that he will complete the season alongside Ollie Bearman.

The Brazilian was already set to compete for Haas in 2027 as the sole rookie on the grid, but the early departure of Esteban Ocon opened the door for him to make an early debut at his home race.

After managing the challenging conditions at Interlagos, Camara gained further experience at the Las Vegas Grand Prix before the team announced that he would continue in his new role for the remainder of the season.

Speaking in Qatar, Camara conceded that while it was likely the right call in the long term, it still was “not easy” to abandon his F2 title challenge – he currently holds a seven-point lead over Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov, with Alpine’s Alex Dunne a further 11 points adrift.

“We know it was a long year in F2 and was a year that we were coming back,” Camara explained. “It was building up and we had this fight at the end, so for sure it was going to be nice to be there fighting these last two weekends.

“In the end it was a decision that probably for the future would make more sense – staying in F1 and being prepared for next year. It was not a decision that was [made in] one day and everything was decided very quickly because it is something that is not an easy one.”

Asked whether he believes there’s a chance he could still secure the title – which would rely on two low-scoring rounds for his competitors – Camara responded: “I think that will be very difficult. It was a year that I worked for that, towards the title and we had a chance to be there fighting.

“It feels a bit sad that I'm not going to be able to fight these two weekends, but like I said, I think for the future it will be something that makes myself more prepared and more ready for everything. It was a tough one.

“I’m just very thankful for everything [Invicta Racing] did for me this year. Without them, I wouldn't be in this position now because I wouldn't be having the opportunities that I'm getting. It was a really enjoyable year and [I will] try to also finish well in F1.”

Camara has had a busy start to his F1 career, enduring a wet weekend in Brazil and a closely fought race in Las Vegas, leaving him hoping for a “calm” outing in Qatar – another circuit he has yet to race at.

Outlining his approach, he said: “I think [I will] really just try to absorb the maximum that I can these two weekends. I think this is something also very rare to have and [I’m] just trying to make the best of it to be prepared for next year.

“I think this weekend will be the most calm one. Obviously no rain, it's more consistent. Here I'm able to have more the same conditions and a normal weekend in that every time you get a better and better track.

“Just improve the track, get more laps and understand everything. Also there are a lot of run-off areas so on that side you can risk a bit more, knowing that if you do a mistake you're not going to crash. I think it's going to be a weekend that will be very nice.”

title: Bearman reflects on new Haas deal and Ferrari hopes
excerpt:
Ollie Bearman has shared his reaction following the long-awaited confirmation that he will continue to drive for Haas in 2027, with the Briton reflecting on his immediate goal going forward while also admitting that, in the long-term, his “dream is to race for Ferrari”.

Despite the expectation being that he would remain with Haas next season, the news had still yet to be officially announced last time out at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, leading Bearman to concede that it was “disappointing” to be at that stage of the campaign without having the situation resolved.

However, it was finally announced just as the F1 paddock arrived in Qatar for the penultimate event of the year that Bearman had re-signed with the American outfit, marking his third full-time season racing for the team.

“We got there in the end,” the 21-year-old explained during media day at the Lusail International Circuit.

“Even though it was very, very sure that I would continue with Haas since forever, it's always a little bit unnerving, especially when we got to a certain stage and you have people on the team asking you what you're doing, and then of course naturally those guys are as a group not fully focused on what's the important thing, which is the on-track stuff. So yeah, everything good, and I'm looking forward to the future.”

Pushed on the goal that he has set for himself and Haas in 2027, Bearman responded: “Well, nothing yet. It depends how fast the car is, right? We're trying to make it as fast as possible, and then we see.

“I think the target for us is to get to the front of the midfield. That's not something that's going to happen overnight or from one season to the next, because this year we haven't been anywhere near to that. But yeah, progress is the target.”

Bearman remains a part of Ferrari’s junior programme and previously made his F1 debut for the Scuderia when he stood in for an unwell Carlos Sainz at the 2024 Saudi Arabian Grand Prix, a race that saw the British driver also score his maiden points with a P7 finish.

Asked if there was confidence that he would get his chance with Ferrari in the future, Bearman said: “I hope so. I would say that I'm here thanks to Ferrari.

Why Bearman's new Haas deal took so long to get over the line

“I don't know, if I didn't get that chance in Jeddah [in 2024], if I would be sitting here right now, so I'm incredibly grateful to Ferrari for the opportunities they gave me, for putting me in the car as an 18-year-old – I think that was a pretty big risk and it paid off.

“They also put me in this Haas car, so the opportunities that they've given me have been amazing and I would love to put the red suit back on one day. I had the feeling, I had a little taste, but my dream is to race for Ferrari.”

For now Bearman stated that his immediate outlook is the “continuation with Haas”, while he also hopes that becoming the most experience driver in the squad – with rookie Rafael Camara joining as his team mate – can prove his worth to the top teams.

“I think it's definitely interesting. It's something to work towards, right?” Bearman said of the leadership role. “If you want to be successful or go anywhere in Formula 1, I think you need to prove that you're capable of leading a team.

“Coming from Formula 2, I was very impressed by Esteban [Ocon] as I joined him as a team mate, the way that he was able to lead the team forward. I certainly learnt a lot from him, and I feel like it's a natural progression.

“It definitely came sooner than I was maybe anticipating to be the most experienced guy in only my third year in F1, but I think it's an exciting prospect and I think the team has definitely gained a lot of trust in the feedback that I give them.

“And on top of that, I also think I've made good progress in that regard as well. If you asked me 12 months ago, am I ready to be the most experienced driver, I would tell you certainly not, categorically no.

“Six months ago, there was a chance, and now I feel like I'm ready to step into that. So yeah, it's exciting – it's exciting times, and I think I can prove to the top teams that I have what it takes to do that. “

title: Norris concedes 2026 ‘certainly not been our finest’ year
excerpt:
McLaren’s Lando Norris believes that the 2026 season has “certainly not been our finest” after failing to defend both the Drivers’ and Teams’ Championships, with the Briton adding that they “wished for a better” year.

The Woking-based outfit entered this season as the top team, having clinched back-to-back constructors’ titles in 2024 and 2025 while Norris took the crown by two points over Max Verstappen last season.

However, setbacks under the latest regulations saw McLaren lose out to Mercedes and Ferrari before they clinched their first victory of the campaign in Hungary. Additional strong performances in the Netherlands, Brazil and Las Vegas have kept them in the battle for P3 with Red Bull, with the two separated by just nine points.

Asked how he reflects on the season ahead of the penultimate round in Qatar, Norris said: “I feel very happy honestly. You can only be as happy as you feel like your own performance has been. I feel like it's been very good for me.

“It doesn't mean I won a load of races, it doesn't mean we're fighting for a championship but that's how F1 is sometimes. You get opportunities and sometimes you don't, but I still feel like I've had a very, very strong year relative to the people you can compare to.

“Of course I wish for more, as does the whole team, we wished for a better season. The team of course also wished that they could put up a better fight in terms of constructors' and also for me to have a chance of fighting again in the drivers'. But you can't win them all.

“We're up against some of the best people in the world, drivers in the world and it's hard to compete at that level every single year. This year has certainly not been our finest, and we do put some of that down to the transition from last year to this year. But my year has been very good otherwise.”

McLaren achieved their second double podium of the season last time out in Las Vegas, where Norris and his team mate Oscar Piastri capitalised on the eventful race to follow winner Verstappen over the line.

The Lusail International Circuit poses a vastly different challenge and was the site of a crucial victory for the Dutchman last season, which took the title fight to the final round. Although Mercedes and Kimi Antonelli have already wrapped up the respective championships, there is plenty for McLaren to fight for in Qatar once again.

“It was a good weekend in Vegas,” Norris explained. “Better than our expectation going in which is always a good thing. Good points for us as a team, which is a good thing, and got more points than Red Bull. In terms of what we wanted to achieve it was a very good weekend actually.

“Still not where we wanted to be and probably still didn't have the pace of what we wanted but this is a different weekend. It's one we know we've performed well at in the past, we also know it's one Red Bull always perform well at. I don't really have any expectations, just have to work hard and try again.

“I feel like I've improved in certain areas and it's always nice coming back to different tracks where it was getting more tense last year. Obviously Vegas was not a good one for us last year and here was certainly not a good one either.

“It's also a race I do enjoy and I feel like I've never really had the result I feel like I should get here, so I'm hoping this weekend I can make up for that.”

title: Facts, stats and trivia ahead of the 2026 Qatar GP
excerpt:
The closing triple header of the 2026 Formula 1 season continues this weekend as the Lusail International Circuit hosts Round 22 on the calendar, the Qatar Grand Prix.

Free Practice 1 and 2 will take place on Friday, November 27, followed by Free Practice 3 and Qualifying on Saturday, November 28, and the Grand Prix itself on Sunday, November 29.

Vital statistics

First Grand Prix – 2021

Track Length – 5.419km

Lap record – 1m 22.384s, Lando Norris, McLaren, 2024

Most pole positions – Max Verstappen (2)

Most wins – Max Verstappen (3)

Trivia – 2021 represented the first time Qatar had ever hosted an F1 race

Pole run to Turn 1 braking point – 403 metres

Overtakes completed in 2025 – 41

Safety Car probability – 75%*

Virtual Safety Car probability – 50%*

Pit stop time loss – 26.17 seconds

*From the previous four races in Qatar

The driver’s verdict

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver: Qatar is full of medium-speed corners and flowing sections. Given that it’s not a huge braking circuit, it’s just about finding the optimum downforce level for the car.

There’s one good overtaking opportunity, and that comes down the lengthy start/finish straight.

The kerbs can be quite punishing, so drivers will need to be careful there, but conversely, as it’s a night race, that will help the tyres a little bit compared to the afternoon heat.

Everything to know about the Lusail International Circuit

Qatar GP polesitters

2025 – Oscar Piastri (McLaren)

2024 – George Russell (Mercedes)*

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2021 – Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

*Max Verstappen set the fastest time in Qualifying but was demoted one place due to a penalty

Qatar GP winners

2025 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2021 – Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

Tyre and strategy insight

“For this race, Pirelli has selected the three hardest compounds in its range: the C1 as hard, the C2 as medium, and the C3 as soft,” reads Pirelli’s weekend preview. “The choice is dictated by the characteristics of the Qatari circuit, which generates a particularly high level of wear, especially on the front-left tyre.

“The circuit features 16 corners and its high level of severity stems from the succession of high-speed turns, which subject the tyres to continuous stress for much of the lap. The relatively smooth track surface and the high track temperatures can encourage graining on all compounds, a phenomenon that further increases wear.

“Despite operating in very demanding conditions, the tyres deliver consistent performance throughout the stint. Experience from previous years has shown that performance degradation remains relatively limited even when wear levels are high.

“To prevent tyres from being used beyond their intended life, managing degradation while placing excessive fatigue on the structure, Pirelli has introduced, in agreement with the FIA, a maximum stint length of 27 laps for each set. As a result, the race will inevitably be a minimum two-stop event for all drivers.

“The maximum lap limit has been increased compared to last year because the 2026 tyres feature a further reinforced construction and the cars generate lower levels of aerodynamic load than their 2025 predecessors.

“The introduction of this restriction, as an alternative to other measures such as increasing minimum starting pressures, will allow drivers to push harder during their stints, reducing the need for pace management.”

Current form

Max Verstappen arrives into the weekend off the back of winning a frenetic Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the result meaning that the Red Bull driver now has an even stronger hold on second place in the drivers’ standings behind the already-crowned World Champion Kimi Antonelli.

Having scored nine consecutive podium finishes during the second half of the season, Verstappen remains one of the favourites in Qatar – particularly given that the Dutchman has triumphed across F1’s last three visits to the Lusail International Circuit.

McLaren have also experienced success at the circuit – with Oscar Piastri taking his first win of any kind during the Sprint in 2023 (see below for this iconic moment) as well as claiming pole position last year – and the squad will be keen to carry some momentum into this weekend after earning a double podium finish in Las Vegas.

Over at Mercedes, the Silver Arrows will be hoping for a better outcome after missing out on a potential win last time out, with Antonelli experiencing an issue on the last lap that dropped him back to P4 while George Russell hit the barriers when trying to overtake Antonelli, leaving him down in ninth.

The Briton also saw his rivalry with Verstappen reignited during the weekend, with both making comments about one another following an incident between them in free practice. Will the dispute have an impact on how the pair go racing in Qatar?

Elsewhere, Ferrari were faced with a difficult situation after contact occurred when Charles Leclerc tried to make a move on Lewis Hamilton, an incident that Leclerc received a 10-second time penalty for. With Team Principal Fred Vasseur stating that the team would “discuss what happened internally” in the days after, it will be interesting to see the approach that the Scuderia take this weekend.

In the midfield battle, meanwhile, Alpine secured a solid haul of points in Las Vegas while Racing Bulls left with none – but the Enstone-based outfit may still struggle to catch up in the fight for P6, given that the gap stands at 27 points. Audi, on the other hand, are only three points away from seventh-placed Haas, meaning that a good outing for the former could see them move up.

Iconic moment

Qatar played host to the Sprint when it made its return to the calendar in 2023 following a one-year hiatus, and the star of the 100km dash was undoubtedly Oscar Piastri, the Australian having taken pole position for the event before making a strong start off the line.

While he faced pressure from George Russell at the restart following a Safety Car period – allowing the Mercedes to ultimately take the lead – Piastri was the one to benefit from a later Safety Car deployment as he surged back into P1 when the action resumed.

From there the McLaren man kept his cool in humid conditions to claim his first victory of any kind in Formula 1.

title: Gabriel Bortoleto lambasts rivals with 'what the f***' question after freak race
excerpt:
Gabriel Bortoleto has told his fellow F1 drivers to "give it a break" with their criticisms of the Las Vegas overtaking fest, asking: "What the f*** do they want?" from grands prix.

An all-time 352 overtakes happened in the Las Vegas GP, where the slipstream and tow were extremely powerful with cars chopping and changing positions multiple times a lap, especially on the Strip into Turn 14 and then on the long run to Turn 1 and through the final left-hand kink.

Whilst some drivers were happy with the style of racing, others, including Max Verstappen, declared that whilst it looked good for TV audiences, his "racer's heart" was against it.

Alex Albon, who missed the race with a mechanical issue, explained that he "got bored" within four laps and that it was a "Formula E" peloton style of racing.

Given the relative split between the field, Bortoleto, who finished 12th for Audi just behind team-mate Nico Hulkenberg in 11th, explained that drivers "need to drive and do [their job].

"I must be honest that maybe because we struggle with the speed on the straights, I was always making overtakes at the last second in the middle of the corner, so for me it was actually quite nice," Bortoleto told media, including RacingNews365.

"Rarely, I made a few moves in the middle of the straight when the other car was running out of battery, but most of the moves I made were with Oliver; for example, we were always in Turn 1 in a super close battle, and I quite enjoyed the race.

"I must say, I wouldn't complain about it, and I think at the same time, we need to give it a break.

"I think some drivers have been complaining when it's not overtaking, when it's overtaking. So what the fuck do they want, you know?

"You need to drive and do your job, and that is it.

"[After the race, I went to talk with Oliver; it was super cool how close the battle was between us, and also with Nico.

"I had a few fights with him, so it was something just bringing back that feeling of overtaking which for a few races, we didn't have."

title: Max Verstappen hit with unexpected Red Bull absence at Qatar Grand Prix
excerpt:
Max Verstappen will work with 2027 race engineer Tom Hart at this weekend's Qatar Grand Prix in a change to the plan for the Gianpiero Lambiase succession.

Over the final six races of the season, starting in the United States, Lambiase and Hart have shared race engineering duties for the four-time champion as preparation for 2027, when Lambiase will leave Red Bull to enter a period of gardening leave before his move to McLaren.

Hart, Verstappen's performance engineer, took over engineering duties for the United States, São Paulo, and Las Vegas Grands Prix, with Lambiase planned to undertake his duties in Mexico City, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi.

However, Lambiase is to miss this weekend's Qatar race with Hart stepping in once again, a team spokesperson confirmed to RacingNews365.

It is understood that Lambiase will miss the race for personal reasons, with no decision being made as yet as to whether he will engineer Verstappen for the final time in the Abu Dhabi season finale.

In Las Vegas, Hart secured his first victory as Verstappen's race engineer, with the Verstappen-Lambiase partnership combining for 74 wins - second only to the Lewis Hamilton-Peter Bonnington Mercedes pairing, which accounted for 83 of Hamilton's 84 wins between 2013 and 2024.

title: Liam Lawson reveals ‘new protocol’ after ‘mentally frustrating’ F1 experience
excerpt:
Liam Lawson is hopeful fuel problems for Racing Bulls are officially a thing of the past.

Liam Lawson has revealed Racing Bulls has introduced a "new protocol" following his late start at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, after a fuel leak left him a lap down before the race had even begun.

The New Zealander was sent out of the pits rather than from his grid slot after mechanics discovered the leak shortly before the start, forcing a complicated repair that could not be completed in time.

It meant Lawson began the race already a full lap behind the field, a problem compounded by a similar fuel-system issue the team had encountered earlier in the season at Monaco.

Lawson eventually finished last, his evening spent isolated from the pack with no cars to race with even a late safety car leaving him comfortably adrift.

Speaking to select media, including RacingNews365, on Qatar media day, Lawson confirmed the team had held discussions on how to catch such issues earlier in future.

Asked if talks had taken place after Las Vegas to discover problems sooner, Lawson said: "Exactly that. Now we have new sort of protocols involved that will stop that happening again, basically, or at least it would be for its own different reasons. So, yeah, we should not have this issue again."

Pushed on what the new protocol actually involves, Lawson explained it was a simple change to the team's fuelling schedule.

"Something that we've just decided to do. It's literally just fuelling the car earlier, so that there's enough time if something like that does happen, we have time to change it all," added Lawson.

Driver

Liam Lawson

New Zealander

30

Liam Lawson details lonely Las Vegas struggle

Lawson also detailed just how isolating the race in Las Vegas became once he was a lap down with no rivals nearby to fight.

"It was so frustrating because I had no tow, like not a single car in sight," detailed Lawson. "So, as a driver, it's really frustrating, especially a race like Vegas. You're not looking out for tyres; you're just flat out.

"So, when you're flat out but you're racing nobody, and you're a lap down, it's a really mentally frustrating race, and I'm just watching the screens the whole time to watch the race, to basically see what's happening, praying for a safety car or something like that.

"And then we got the safety car, and unfortunately, didn't have enough time to catch the field. So, even more frustrating again to be on the lead lap, but still 25 seconds back, so overall it was just frustrating.

"And then to see sort of the performance of the car afterwards as well, and see the pace that we had, yeah, it was frustrating."

title: Rafael Camara explains decision to abandon F2 title challenge
excerpt:
Rafael Camara has explained his decision to abandon his Formula 2 title challenge to race in the final two F1 grands prix of the season.

Camara is currently leading the FIA F2 standings from Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov by seven points, having won the last race the series held, the second feature race in Azerbaijan.

Camara was then announced as being a 2027 Haas F1 driver, replacing Esteban Ocon, who was stood down following FP2 at the Mexico City Grand Prix, and who has now formally left the team.

Ryo Hirakawa deputised for Ocon in Mexico, bagging a point, before Camara was given the nod for his home race in Sao Paulo and in Las Vegas, but a decision had not been made about the final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, where FIA F2 will hold its final two rounds of the season.

Drivers are not allowed to compete in both F1 and F2 on the same weekend, with the exception of FP1 rookie driver sessions, with Oliver Bearman being withdrawn from the F2 weekend at the 2024 Saudi Arabian GP, despite being on pole, after Carlos Sainz was struck down with appendicitis and Bearman called up for his debut with Ferrari.

The decision was taken after Las Vegas to stand Camara down from F2 duties to allow him an extra two grands prix to prepare for his full-time debut in 2027, with Tsolov now 11 points clear of Alex Dunne in third place at the top of the standings.

Reflecting on the decision, Camara, the reigning FIA F3 champion, conceded that he was a "bit sad" not to be able to potentially add the FIA F2 title to his CV.

The likes of Charles Leclerc, George Russell, Oscar Piastri, and Gabriel Bortoleto are drivers who have won GP3/F3 and GP2/F2 back-to-back before earning F1 promotion.

"It is a bit sad that the whole year has been working for that, and in the end, we will not do these two races," Camara told media, including RacingNews365.

"For sure, unless something crazy happens [I will not be champion], and it was not easy to decide.

"It is a bit sad when you want to do these two races, but on the other hand, I think it is something very useful to do [Qatar and Abu Dhabi] in FP1."

Speaking about his baptism of fire in F1 after the rain in Sao Paulo and the slipstream fest of Las Vegas, Camara spoke of the useful nature of banking knowledge for the future.

"Every weekend has been very intense, and I was really able to learn a lot," he said.

"With the rain and all the weather in Interlagos, it was crazy, and going to Las Vegas, another easy track, but a particular one as it is very cold; you have experience with the tyres and trying to switch them on.

"That makes a huge difference, and I think having these two weekends was very useful for the future, but I think it'll be a bit harder here in Qatar."

[Article continues below]

Being on 'the same page'

Further explaining about the adjustment from working with an F2 team to an F1 outfit, Camara spoke of being on "the same page" with the team.

"Every weekend you learn and understand more about how everything works," he said.

"In F2, you obviously have a small group of people that you're working with, and here is quite a lot.

"So I think that understanding these processes and making sure you know what to do and that you're on the same page with everyone is something useful for next year.

"Every weekend you understand things more and then you're just more positive, and it makes your life easier when you're in the car."

title: Lewis Hamilton refuses to share information after crunch Charles Leclerc talks
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has refused to share any information regarding the outcome of the latest round of talks with warring team-mate Charles Leclerc.

In Las Vegas, the two Ferraris collided at Turn 7, with Hamilton being spun around by Leclerc, who then incurred a 10-second penalty, and the wrath of Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur, who demanded to speak to the Monegasque as soon as he got out of the car.

Vasseur branded the incident as "unacceptable" and felt that the warring drivers were becoming "unmanageable" following other incidents at the start of the Italian GP when Leclerc put Hamilton into the gravel and then again in Mexico City, where Leclerc attacked Hamilton at Turn 4 on the opening lap, with both drivers losing out on a likely one-two victory.

After Mexico, the pair, along with Vasseur sat down for talks in Sao Paulo, which were revealed to be positive, but before the spat in Las Vegas.

Now, the trio have held a further round of talks, in which Leclerc revealed he was unable to comment on potential sanctions.

Hamilton also kept his cards close to his chest, except to reveal the latest round of talks had been "good."

"We had internal discussions," Hamilton began to media, including RacingNews365, before fielding a question about if he could share any more information.

"No," he replied. "Everything stays internal," before revealing that the discussions had been good.

"It's been positive. Charles and I sat here earlier and had a good discussion."

When then asked about the potential sanctions, Hamilton indicated that it was for Vasseur to decide whether anything formal was written down on paper.

"It is for Fred to decide," he said.

"Ultimately, I made my point clear already about them, so there is not really much more to say.

"I've said my piece, and my point hasn't really changed."

[Article continues below]

Hamilton on potential Ferrari rules

Turning to how the potential rules would work in a grand prix with unique scenarios, Hamilton spoke of using his instinct to judge situations.

"You can never cover everything because every scenario is different," he said.

"But you can definitely you can go through every single race, bit by bit, corner by corner, and discuss things with Charles and I have.

"But there's always going to be something new that you maybe haven't foreseen, but also you have to use your instinct, and you also always, at the core of it, always have to have the team.

"I mean, just speaking for myself, when I'm driving, when I'm attacking whoever it is on track, I'm always thinking: 'Okay, how is this going to impact everybody behind me, team-wise?'

"So I really do try to be as responsible as I can and make the best decision when I am attacking."

title: Charles Leclerc explains why he is 'not allowed' to address Lewis Hamilton clash sanctions
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has explained why he is "not allowed" to discuss the "solutions" Ferrari has adopted to his spate of on-track skirmishes with Lewis Hamilton.

The pair clashed for the third time this season at the recent Las Vegas Grand Prix, with Leclerc spinning Hamilton at Turn 7 in Sin City.

It earned the Monegasque driver a 10-second time penalty and cost the Scuderia valuable points. He crossed the line in sixth, but dropped to P10 when his punishment was applied, whilst his team-mate was promoted to seventh.

It comes following an incident at Monza and a first-lap battle at the Mexico City Grand Prix when running first and second. The latter threw away a likely victory and potentially a one-two finish.

The aftermath led to crunch talks between Leclerc, Hamilton and Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur at the subsequent round in São Paulo, but the fallout post-Las Vegas has been more severe.

Vasseur called the collision "unacceptable" and acknowledged that the partnership between his drivers was becoming "unmanageable", even hinting at regret over pairing them together at the Italian team.

Asked about the situation in the Qatar Thursday drivers' press conference, Leclerc kept his cards close to his chest.

"I mean, Fred already talked on the radio telling me he wanted to speak to me before going to the media, and so I obviously knew where Fred was standing, and as a driver, you've got to accept that," Leclerc told media, including RacingNews365.

When then asked why the accidents keep happening, Leclerc indicated that a "solution" needed to be found.

"At the end of the day, we are two very strong drivers that want to finish one ahead of the other," he began.

"Unfortunately, recently, whether it's in [Las Vegas], or Monza or, Mexico, there have been a bit too many events of those lately, and we need to find a solution as a team to make sure that these kinds of things don't happen again. That's it."

The Monegasque then indicated he was "not allowed" to comment further, owing to the talks being an internal matter within the team.

"I'm not going to disclose that," he said when asked for what a possible solution would be.

"I mean, I'm not allowed to anyway. So, yeah, I cannot go into the detail of that."

Leclerc then batted away a question about the rules of engagement, insisting he "cannot disclose" whether they would change for Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

[Article continues below]

Leclerc vs Hamilton

Then, speaking about the intensity of racing with Hamilton, Leclerc explained that the scrutiny was higher than with Marcus Ericsson, Sebastian Vettel, Carlos Sainz, or Oliver Bearman in the sister car as previous team-mates.

"I feel there is a level of scrutiny that is higher than ever for sure," he said.

"There might be some valid reasons for that. Some others may be a bit less, but at the end of the day, it doesn't really matter.

"I think what's most important is that we find a solution going forward, and that we try to avoid these kinds of things as much as possible."

title: George Russell offers first response to scathing Max Verstappen taunts
excerpt:
George Russell has offered his first public response to the taunts Max Verstappen threw at him after the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

In Sin City, the feud between the two reignited after an incident in third practice at the end of the Strip, where the two tangled, leading Russell to claim that Verstappen's actions were akin to "screwing a person over," and that he "does this week in, week out, with everybody accepting it.

"I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walking around like they're bigger and better than everyone else.

“Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

Verstappen then kept his powder dry until after winning the race, when Russell hit a barrier on Lap 48 of 50 whilst trying to pass Kimi Antonelli for second, and fell to ninth.

In the post-race press conference, Verstappen then declared that Russell was not bothering him as he was "so far below my level" and that "karma is a bitch. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror, and I saw what was happening.

"I was like 'fantastic, my day is only getting better'. And when I crossed the line in first, my day was complete."

Reacting for the first time to Verstappen's attack in the Qatar drivers' press conference, Russell played a straight bat.

"I don't really have much to say, to be honest," he told media, including RacingNews365.

"I found some of the comments post-race quite amusing, but at the end of the day, he drove an incredible race, and won it, so he can afford to say what he wants, really.

"From my side, I am moving on."

When then asked if there was anything he wanted to say back to Verstappen, Russell declined.

"No, not really to be honest. I guess I stand by what I said after practice, but he was the one who went out and won the race. I didn't.

"So I am sure he had a bit of a laugh about it, and it was reasonably amusing, so from my side, it is a new race weekend, and I will try to focus on the driving and move on."

title: McLaren address major upcoming F1 change after 'anomaly' problem
excerpt:
The FIA will introduce permanent F1 stewards starting next year in the hope of fixing inconsistencies that have generated complaints from the drivers.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has hailed the FIA for the introduction of full-time stewards to oversee F1.

The move comes after years of complaints from drivers over inconsistencies in stewarding decisions, with the figures constantly rotating race to race.

The FIA is seeking to put a stop to such concerns from the drivers with a permanent panel to draw from.

It outlined that a "phased introduction" is expected during the 2027 season before an expansion in 2028, a move that McLaren has embraced.

“We welcome these kind of changes,” Stella told media including RacingNews365. “We have been in conversation with the FIA.

“At the level of professionalism that we have in F1 nowadays, it's a bit of an anomaly that such a key stakeholder is not at the same level of professional status.

“I would say very, very capable individuals, very competent. But we need to give the stewards, the board of stewards, the possibility to act at the best of their abilities.

“Which means continuity, which means all the kind of best practices that you put in place when you approach that with a full professional approach.

“So we welcome this news.”

What will change?

Away from race weekends, the permanent stewards are expected to take on a broader remit, reviewing incident trends across the season, recommending updates to sporting regulations and driving guidelines, and mentoring trainee officials coming through the FIA's High Performance Programme.

The reform also reflects a practical need: a standing body of professional officials would give the FIA the resources to support its other single-seater championships, not just Formula 1.

Other series offer a template. IndyCar has run a permanent stewarding model since 2016, while Supercars has long relied on a fixed Driving Standards Advisor.

Both have delivered more predictable rulings, though observers note such structures have occasionally drawn accusations of entrenched bias or overly personal interpretations building up over time.

That tension is not new to the FIA itself, which has previously argued that a fully static panel risks being accused of favouring or targeting particular drivers and teams across an entire campaign.

The hybrid approach for 2027, retaining rotating and regional panel members alongside the new full-time appointees, appears designed to guard against exactly that criticism.

title: Lando Norris confirms key McLaren meeting topic on shocking error anniversary
excerpt:
Lando Norris has confirmed that McLaren's disastrous 2025 Qatar Grand Prix strategy call will come up in his pre-weekend meeting with the team, a year on since the error derailed his title bid in Lusail.

The Briton finished fourth at last year's race after McLaren opted to leave both him and Oscar Piastri out on track during a lap seven safety car, caused by a clash between Nico Hulkenberg and Pierre Gasly.

With a mandatory 25-lap tyre stint limit in force, almost the entire field, led by Max Verstappen, pitted for free under the neutralisation, leaving McLaren's pair committed to two further green-flag stops and stranded in traffic.

Verstappen went on to win the race, while Norris slipped behind Carlos Sainz to finish fourth. The call cut his championship lead over the Dutchman from 24 points to just 12 heading into the Abu Dhabi finale.

Team principal Andrea Stella later admitted it was a tactical misjudgement, with McLaren simply not expecting so many rivals to pit so early.

Asked what discussions had taken place to avoid a repeat, Norris told select media, including RacingNews365, that he had not dwelt on it.

"I've not thought a bit about it at all, to be honest. There were obviously conversations that we had last year, and I'm sure the team have been having discussions. And it's something that we'll probably speak about later today when I have my meetings upstairs."

"But the simple thing is, it's still not as easy as just saying we would have boxed last year. If we would have boxed, we still would have been stuck in the pit lane, a lot more people would have come out ahead of us, and it wasn't a guarantee we were getting back past them. So, yeah, it's still not as simple as what everyone says."

"But of course, we'll try and see how we can do a better job than we did last season."

title: Honda deny problem with Fernando Alonso engine after mysterious issue
excerpt:
Honda has been unable to identify any problems with the power unit in Fernando Alonso's Aston Martin after he retired from the Las Vegas Grand Prix at the final corner.

Alonso pulled into the pit lane at the end of the 50-lap race in Sin City instead of taking the chequered flag, bemoaning an issue with his engine.

However, in the days since, the Japanese marque has still not been able to detect anything wrong with the unit, as it stated shortly after the race.

"We have checked all the data we have now, and during maintenance, we also checked the engine physically," said Shintaro Orihara, Honda's trackside general manager and chief engineer, to media, including RacingNews365.

"At this moment, we haven't found any issues with the engine from the data or from the maintenance. But we will check on Friday how the engine works on this track."

Alonso, who is missing media day at the Qatar Grand Prix as he recovers from a viral infection, is due to be back in his AMR26 for FP2 at the Lusail International Circuit, with Jak Crawford deputising in FP1.

Despite their accounts being at odds, Orihara was keen to express how much Honda "respect" the feedback provided by Alonso.

"We carefully analysed his comments, and we also respect his comments. That's why we checked all the data, and we also checked the engine condition," he said.

"But from the data, at the moment we haven't seen any issues. But as I mentioned, we should check again on Friday to get some feedback from Fernando."

[Article continues below]

What might be causing the disparity in accounts?

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit is an outlier on the F1 calendar and, due to the energy-poor, high-speed nature of the track, it is not a happy hunting ground for the underpowered Honda engine.

That paucity was exacerbated by the slipstream-fest that was experienced in Nevada, amplifying the shortcomings of the power unit.

"In Las Vegas, it's difficult to analyse how engine performance affects car speed; there is a lot of the tow effect, and also different energy management across two cars," Orihara added. "So our metrics say power itself is okay, but probably we should check carefully on these tracks again...

"Probably, this year, our engine performance is not enough to satisfy or give confidence to the drivers, and then probably they feel the engine performance is not great."

Mike Krack, Aston Martin's chief trackside officer, also defended the situation, stressing caution about jumping to conclusions over the disparity from the information and contradictory accounts from Alonso and Honda.

He detailed how the increased energy usage under the 2026 F1 power unit regulations can make it confusing for a driver to work out what is combustion power and what is from the battery.

"We need to be careful because the K [MGU-K] power is so much higher that as soon as you have even a small variation in K, it could feel like the ICE [internal combustion engine] — and you have different K power in different places," said Krack.

"So very often, for the drivers, it's much more difficult to judge than it used to be in the past. And I think some of it is coming from there."

title: Arvid Lindblad makes Qatar F1 prediction that amplifies Las Vegas 'hurt'
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad spun into retirement on Lap 20 of the Las Vegas Grand Prix — but this is why it "hurts" so much.

Arvid Lindblad expects F1's leading teams to pull clear again at the Qatar Grand Prix, making it all the harder for the Racing Bulls rookie to accept losing a rare chance to fight for a podium in Las Vegas.

Lindblad started fifth and climbed to third in the opening stages, as the strength of the slipstream on the Las Vegas Strip allowed him to take the fight to the front-runners.

The tow proved to be the dominant factor over the 50-lap race in Sin City, with 352 overtakes and 35 changes for the lead — the former of which is an F1 record.

Aided by battery management requirements on one of the most energy-poor circuits on the calendar, the peloton-style yo-yo racing was not to everyone's liking, but Lindblad thoroughly enjoyed his taste of it.

"I didn't expect it to be quite like that," the 19-year-old told media, including RacingNews365, after his retirement.

"I had a feeling before the race that it was going to be a bit more like a go-kart race than normal, but I think it's great for the sport.

"I'm sure many of the drivers will say that it's not the most organic racing and whatever.

"There have been many flaws with this power unit, but it's worked quite well at this track because it's made the tows so powerful. So I think, for me, it was pretty cool. I enjoyed it."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Arvid Lindblad

British

41

Losing the chance to 'do something special'

Lindblad was running sixth on lap 20 when he spun while warming his tyres behind the safety car and could not get going again.

He described an unusual gear change as he eased onto the throttle, but took responsibility for the spin and his ultimate retirement.

With Qatar and Abu Dhabi to come, Lindblad believes Las Vegas was his best chance to race in that company before his rookie season ends.

"We'll be back in Qatar, being the standard, off the top teams," the Racing Bulls driver said. "You'll have the standard; they'll drive away in the race, and that's the way it's going to be.

"That's the way it's going to be in Abu Dhabi. That's what it's like on a normal circuit. This is not a normal circuit, and the chance to race and do something special.

"I fully believe a top five was available. And if I raced well and I was smart, who knows, maybe even slightly more?

"And I think that's the part that hurts because, yeah, fine, I can race for P8, P9, P10 in the next couple of races; that's fantastic.

"But it's not often you get to race for P3, P4, P5 in a midfield car in your rookie season. I think that's what hurts me."

title: Fernando Alonso to miss key Qatar GP duties due to viral infection
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso will be absent from media day at the Qatar Grand Prix as he continues to recover from a viral infection, Aston Martin has confirmed.

Alonso contracted the virus over the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend, the previous round, and will therefore spend Thursday resting and further recuperating as he readies himself for track action tomorrow at the Lusail International Circuit.

Whilst the Silverstone-based squad did not confirm that the FIA had permitted him to miss his press duties, it is accepted as standard when a driver is unwell.

A spokesperson for Aston Martin said: "Fernando will miss media day today as he continues to recover from a viral infection contracted towards the end of the Las Vegas GP weekend. He is recovering well, and is planned to return to the paddock on Friday."

Whilst the two-time F1 drivers' champion is therefore expected to be present tomorrow, he will not be in the cockpit of his AMR26 for FP1 anyway, with Jak Crawford deputising for the session.

Lance Stroll missed media day at the São Paulo Grand Prix earlier this month for a similar reason, with the rigours of the F1 calendar affecting drivers and others working in the paddock as the season draws towards a close.

Alonso was absent from his Thursday press session at the Japanese Grand Prix at the third round of the season due to the birth of his son.

title: Ferrari boss sets Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc clear target after latest clash
excerpt:
Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur has called on Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc to bring both cars home with a "solid result" at the Qatar Grand Prix after the latter spun his team-mate in Las Vegas.

The pair were fighting for sixth when Leclerc tried to pass Hamilton up the inside at Turn 7 in Sin City.

The stewards held Leclerc responsible for the collision and gave him a 10-second penalty that dropped him to P10 at the chequered flag. Hamilton recovered to finish seventh despite a 10-second penalty of his own for passing Lando Norris off the track.

Vasseur described Leclerc's mistake as “completely unacceptable” after the race. He said Ferrari had reminded both drivers to think of the team as they raced each other in Las Vegas, having already sat down with them in Brazil to discuss what happened in Mexico City.

The first flashpoint came at Monza in September, when Hamilton took to the gravel at the opening chicane and told Ferrari over the radio that Leclerc had pushed him off. Leclerc later acknowledged he could have given Hamilton more room.

In Mexico City, both Ferraris ran wide at Turn 4 as Leclerc challenged pole-sitter Hamilton for the lead on the opening lap. Leclerc crossed the grass and emerged ahead, earning a five-second penalty, while Max Verstappen passed Hamilton on the exit. Verstappen went on to win by less than a second from Hamilton, with Leclerc fourth.

"We head to Qatar determined to respond as a team and deliver the kind of weekend we expect from ourselves,” Vasseur said.

"Lusail is very different to Las Vegas, with its long sequences of high-speed corners."

Teams will have to factor Friday’s running into their plans for Sunday. The tyre mileage limit applies across the weekend, and each driver will need at least three sets to cover the 57-lap race.

"The 27-lap limit for each set will also make the tyre allocation and strategy management unique for this weekend," the Ferrari boss added.

"We have three practice sessions to prepare the car, and our objective is clear: maximise every part of the weekend to the highest possible standard and bring home a solid result with both cars."

title: Complete F1 2027 confirmed driver line-ups
excerpt:
Following the confirmation that Oliver Bearman will remain at Haas for the 2027 F1 campaign, the grid for next season has now been finalised.

Like Valtteri Bottas before him, weeks of speculation over the British driver's future can now be put to rest — for now, at least.

The 21-year-old will stay with the American team next year, although no further details about his new contract have been disclosed.

Bearman was always broadly expected to stay put, but recent talks with Alpine's Flavio Briatore and delays in getting the deal with Haas over the line fanned the flames of uncertainty.

At the previous round, in Las Vegas, the British driver voiced his "disappointment" over the process dragging on, with his camp and Haas understood to have been at odds on key issues in the negotiations, such as salary and length of extension.

To further muddy the waters, it is believed that Bearman and his team were seeking assurances from Ferrari, where he was a junior driver, over his future with the Scuderia in F1.

Nonetheless, he will race for Haas next season at the least, with the hopes of joining the Italian squad further down the road.
